en: Alas, would they kick him down,
My steed Taytoru?
Six Cities and Margilan—
Malice lurked in their eyes,
Crookedness lurked in their words.
If their strength allowed, they would destroy me;
They were bent on striking me.
Deceit lurked in their words,
Mischief lurked in their eyes.
If fate allowed, these people
Were bent on ruining me.
Kökchö, khan of the Kazakhs,
Was khan of the Kangdy,
A man of sacred virtue.
Kökchö's son Ümötöy
Had an even greater score to settle.
Jamgyrchy of the Eshtek
Still had an ancient score to settle.
Hero Töshtük, Eleman's son,
He too had a score to settle.
If someone interferes with my horse,
Let me die before my appointed death.
If someone comes to no good,
And blocks my horse's path,
I was a soul dead long ago.
Letting them oppress me meanwhile,
How can I remain alive?
A whole group of those who interfere
Let me offer up as a sacrifice.
If someone interferes with my horse,
Let me offer him up as a sacrifice.
If someone interferes with my horse,
Let me descend upon his head,
Let me scatter his four kinds of livestock.
Let me raid all his mares.
If the old wretch comes near,
Let me strike his brains out,
And then exact
A reckoning for his long-past deeds.
Weeping like this, all alone,
Standing and shrieking in tears,
What wish can I attain?
Rather than suffer humiliation alive,
Let me die like this."
Her thoughts torn with sorrow,
Tears pouring from her eyes;
From her unhappy currant-like eyes
Tears streamed a whip's length.
From her dear quail-like eyes
Tears fell in separate drops.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Her dear hair, thick as a girth,
Bound snugly on her crown.
Saying, 'My Semetey will wear it,'
The marten-fur hat she had been making
She pressed onto her head.
The golden-cheeked battle-axe,
The heirloom left by her noble one,
She fastened snugly at her wrist.
Formerly, Manas the leopard,
Having grown into a mighty man,
The equal of heroic sons,
A lion supported by the Patron,
All twelve parts of his body sound;
Where Akkula had not run or walked,
Not a single patch of ground remained;
That had not heard his battle cry,
Not a single people remained.
When he visited Medina,
When he journeyed to Mecca,
Receiving a letter from the khan-khoja,
Receiving a blessing from the caliph;
Called the Illustrious,
With lion Bakay as his companion,
And his soul-companion Ajybay of the Argyn khan,
A lion such as he;
When he turned back toward Islam,
When he set out from Mecca,
At the pass of Munaryk,
In the desert of Mediyan,
For the gray-maned hero visited by Khizr,
Mighty blades were found.
Six blades bestowed as he wished
Were found from the unseen world.
Of blade-flat Sary-Talaa,
They appeared in the very midst.
Among swords, the very finest,
Zulpukor, acquired by Manas—
When he scattered the unbelievers' livestock,
When he launched a holy campaign against Kakan,
Into dark, brooding Beijing,
When he entered straight and thrust his spear,
The diverse Manchus, the many Chinese,
When he slaughtered them all to the last;
Against the Black Kalmyks and Mongols,
When he fought a fierce war;
Twelve mighty khans died,
Twelve hosts of troops died,
Lions Almambet and Chubak died,
The finest of the sixty,
The most precious of the forty companions,
Heroes Serek and Syrgak died.
Entering Kakan, suffering loss,
Across the ridge of his backbone,
With a white jezail and red plume,
By Kongurbay, Alööke's son,
His back was pierced open.
Reaching Talas alive,
When your magnanimous Manas died,
Kanykey was left in mourning.
All the countless riches,
When those dogs scattered and divided them,
When your sister-in-law suffered humiliation,
The merciless torment,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykey,
Had she not brought it with her?
Zulpukor, left by noble Manas,
Saying, 'My descendant will need it,'
Had she not brought it with her?
Zulpukor, left by Manas,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykey
Hung across her shoulder blades.
The old one, with golden collar, copper sleeves,
Double mail, with lark-eye rings,
The fine, becoming cotton coat,
Your poor sister-in-law Kanykey
Pulled on over herself.
The Gray Belt that fell from the sky
For the exceptionally fortunate hero
Had appeared on the level steppe.
For the hero visited by Khizr,
It had appeared in a place of distress.
Red-whipped Shypshaydar
Was Sooronduk's son,
Almambet's maternal uncle;
Giant Tiken, Börüköz's son—
The palm-sized realm of Islam
Had no strength to match those two.
At that time, troubled were
The thoughts of Almambet and Chubak.
When they saw the pair's appearance,
They cried out in tears,
The children of the Muslim people.
When the two giants came in,
Ruling Andijan,
A khan like Aykojo died,
And sixty champions died as well.
The sovereign with the mighty ancestral spirit
Watched from a hill,
His battle cry splitting stone.
Bakay at his side
He kept troubling,
Saying, 'Joust with those two.'
At that time the Gray Belt
Descended from the sky.
When he cried out and fastened it at his waist,
To the dearly born lord
The Forty Hidden Saints became companions.
When he shouted and fastened it at his waist,
The White Holy Man came and offered his hand.
When he journeyed on a distant road,
Six saints opened the way.
The merciless strife,
Had she not brought it with her?
Weeping piteously to the one God,
Dedicating it to her precious Semetey,
Had she not brought it with her?
Saying, 'Leaving it behind would be hard,'
Saying, 'It is an object left by his father Manas,'
Weeping piteously to the one God,
Dedicating it to her forlorn Semetey,
Had she not brought it with her?
The Gray Belt left by her lord Manas
She fitted snugly at her waist,
Concealing that she was a woman.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Now became a man.
Your precious, unfortunate sister-in-law,
Grieving for her dead husband,
Dressed herself in men's clothes.
The eight khans lying ahead,
She knew, would become enemies.
Almambet's Syrbarang
She hung across her shoulder blades.
Almambet's Syrbarang—
Let me tell of Syrbarang.
When one went out with Syrbarang slung on,
It was the mirror of one's shoulder blades;
When one entered a clash with the enemy,
It was solace for one's entrusted soul.
With thick muzzle, Apple-Head,
Not distinguishing far from near,
Not breaking down in twelve days,
Almambet's Syrbarang
She hung across her shoulder blades.
Inside a rawhide saddlebag,
The never-diminishing ammunition
She loaded onto Akborchuk.
The bright-red steel Lacquered Spear
She took up at a slant.
The helmet of blue iron
She lifted and put on her head.
The banner swayed in her hand,
All the keen steel equipment
Flashing in its proper place.
No one could recognize her as a woman.
Tall of body, broad of shoulder,
Both champion and lion,
Racing a horse while a widow,
Your accomplished sister-in-law was this hero.
Taytoru, who would race,
With hoe-like hooves and broad rump,
Was a steed of the open country.
Saying, 'I entrust it to fate,' without pausing,
Your mountain-like sister-in-law
Of the courser Taytoru
Tied the forelock with blue silk,
And bound his tail with white silk.
Your sister-in-law with the hero's frame
A great lead rope two fathoms long
Selected and fastened on.
A white halter braided in the okoro pattern,
A halter fitting Taytoru,
She chose a strong one and secured it.
Your sister-in-law led him tirelessly.
Akborchuk beneath her
She rode at a gallop like a sheep.
Before the eight khans in Bukhara,
Your sister-in-law brought him, leading him.
Looking neither up nor down,
Your sister-in-law never thought, 'I shall die.'
Without looking around,
Your sister-in-law did not spare her life at all.
She resolved to start trouble.
If someone interfered with her horse,
Your sister-in-law resolved to make a spectacle.
Her breast could not contain her many cares;
Your sister-in-law's tears streamed in ten directions.
"This very year my elder is ninety-five,
My saint who bore a mountain-like sovereign.
At the sight of her, my heart is content.
I have no Mecca but my mother.
My river, whose expanse is like a lake,
Whom I carried on my broad back,
My saint whom I brought from Talas.
When I cherish her, my belly is full.
I have no Mecca but my mother.
My venerable white lady,
Let me go to my mother,
Let me receive my mother's blessing.
My venerable white lady, my sacred mother,
Let me go to my mother.
If my mother does not give her blessing,
Why should I race Taytoru?
Without receiving my mother's blessing,
How can I go to Bukhara?"
